Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Mali's 2024 Code de Procédure Pénale requires Officers of Judicial Police (OPJs) at stations to draft procès-verbaux (PVs) immediately on the spot, signed on each page by OPJ and witnesses, with originals transmitted directly to the Prosecutor. Physical registers (coté et paraphé) are mandated for custody logs. No mention of digital drafting or electronic signatures for initial recording. Monthly reports on case files ("dossiers") are sent, but initial capture is paper-based. Recent digital initiatives (e.g., SIG-DJ 2025 for judicial dossier management, WAPIS 2015 for data centralization, online casier judiciaire 2026) focus on higher-level justice systems, converting existing paper data or central storage, not station-level recording. US State Dept 2023 report notes poor record-keeping but no digital at police level; rural areas face same issues plus access challenges. In francophone Africa, rural police rely on handwritten PVs; no rural-specific digital pilots found. Thus, rural police stations record case files, complaints, incidents on paper.

revision_notes: Fetched the cited Code de Procédure Pénale text directly: it confirms handwritten, page-signed procès-verbaux and paper custody registers (registre d'écrou) at station level, with no provision for digital capture. The cited US State Dept PDF could not be fetched (server blocked the request) but is corroborated by a 2024 child-protection practice guide (BICE) describing gendarmerie/commissariat staff consulting paper 'main courante' and 'registre d'écrou' logs, confirming the paper-based finding independently. The WAPIS source confirms centralisation happens by converting existing paper police data into digital format at a national data centre (DACORE), not by digitising capture at the station. A July 2025 article on Mali's new criminal procedure code (in force since December 2024) and judicial reform programme (PRODEJ 2025-2034) shows digitalisation efforts remain focused on higher courts and case-management software (SIG-DJ), not rural police stations. No evidence found of any rural police station using digital capture. Score confirmed at 1 (Entirely paper).
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Mali record complaints, incidents and case files entirely on paper. The Code de Procédure Pénale (Law No. 2024-028, in force since December 2024) requires Officers of Judicial Police to draft procès-verbaux by hand on the spot, signed page-by-page, with paper custody registers (registre d'écrou, main courante) maintained at the station and originals transmitted physically to the Prosecutor. National initiatives such as WAPIS (which converts existing paper police records into a centralised digital database) and the 2025 SIG-DJ judicial case-management platform operate at a higher administrative level, converting or centralising paper data rather than digitising capture at the point of service. No evidence indicates any digital data capture at rural police station level.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices and village declaration points in Mali primarily use paper-based forms for birth registration, with parents submitting notifications from health facilities or home births to local council centers. High national coverage (90%) achieved through extensive network (8000 points), community agents, free services. Digital CRVS software exists nationally (commercial off-the-shelf), but no evidence of routine electronic entry at most rural points-of-service; likely paper collected and later digitized/aggregated. Plans to expand digital processes, digitize records, leverage digital tools for remote areas indicate emerging digital elements/pilots/donor efforts. Key barriers: poor rural connectivity/electricity, insecurity, vast territory. National CRVS strategy ambitious (2018-2022+), but rural reality lags with paper predominant at point-of-service. Disparities noted in remote/conflict areas.

revision_notes: Fetched the cited AfDB/COMESA CRVS digitalisation assessment (2023), which supports the general characterisation of low facility-level digitalisation across African CRVS systems. Fresh searches found the February 2024 relaunch of Mali's sovereign RAVEC/'Mali Kura Biométrie' system and the creation (February 2025) of a new Agence nationale de Sécurisation des actes d'état civil, plus a July 2025 civil-society sensitisation workshop explicitly stating that 'digitalisation [is] encore insuffisante malgré des avancées notables', particularly in rural areas. These all confirm that digitalisation remains centred on the national identity/RAVEC database and central data-processing centre (CTEDEC), not on capture at rural civil registry offices, which continue to rely on paper declarations. Score confirmed at 1 (Entirely paper).
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices and village declaration points in Mali continue to rely on paper forms for recording births, deaths and marriages at the point of service, submitted by parents or local agents to council-level centres. The national identity system (RAVEC, relaunched as the sovereign 'Mali Kura Biométrie' platform in February 2024) and a newly created Agence nationale de Sécurisation des actes d'état civil (established February 2025) centralise and secure civil-status data, but this digitalisation occurs at national processing centres rather than at rural points of service. A July 2025 government-linked sensitisation workshop on civil registration modernisation explicitly acknowledged that digitalisation remains insufficient, especially in rural areas, where poor connectivity, electricity access and insecurity remain barriers.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Mali predominantly use paper-based recording for attendance, enrollment, grades, and admin data. A 2024 study on Malian schools (basic education level) found 90% of administrative tasks, including student enrollment in paper registers or Excel, student dossiers as physical files, teacher records in registers, are manual. No evidence of digital recording at school level; EMIS exists at national level with paper collection from schools then centralized entry (ADEA peer review 2017 notes resource shortages, delays). Recent digital platforms (e.g., web-based for registration/attendance) appear urban/pilot-focused; rural schools lack infrastructure (no networks, electricity issues). World Bank/GPE projects emphasize access/kits, not school digital records. Score 1: entirely paper-based at rural facility level.

revision_notes: Fetched the KalanGest study (Dec 2024), which confirms the school-level picture: it describes a single-school pilot (Debou Gneri) of a new PHP-based administrative tool, framed as a novel decolonisation effort, implying paper remains the norm elsewhere. One of the four originally cited sources (a Wikipedia ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 page) is irrelevant to the variable and appears to be a stray/erroneous citation; it has been dropped from the verified source list. Found and fetched Mali's official Annuaire Statistique de l'Enseignement Primaire 2023-2024 (Ministry of Basic Education, published September 2024), which describes the national statistical campaign: paper forms ('fiches') are revised, sent out to schools, completed by hand, physically collected, and only then entered into the STATEDUC2 database at the regional education directorate (DREPPNF) level — confirming that data capture at the school itself remains paper-based, with digitisation happening at a higher administrative tier, consistent with the variable's scope guidance. Score confirmed at 1 (Entirely paper).
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Mali record attendance, enrolment, grades and administrative data by hand on paper at the facility level. The Ministry of Basic Education's own statistical methodology, described in the Annuaire Statistique de l'Enseignement Primaire 2023-2024 (published September 2024), confirms that data collection forms ('fiches') are physically distributed to and completed by schools, then collected and only entered into the national STATEDUC2 database at the regional education directorate, not at the school itself. Small-scale pilot software tools (such as KalanGest, tested at a single basic school in 2024) exist but are not in general use. Rural schools generally lack the network infrastructure and reliable electricity needed for point-of-service digital recording.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (CSComs) in Mali predominantly use paper-based registers and forms for patient data recording at the point of service. Community health workers (ASCs) compile paper monthly reports from service registers and deliver them in person to CSComs, where staff review and enter aggregated data into the national DHIS2 system.Health Data Collaborative Mopti case study DHIS2 has been national since 2016, covering most districts, but relies on manual paper inputs from facilities, with data entry at facility/district level, not point-of-care.Gavi ZDLH Digital pilots include DISC-Mali smartphone app for CHWs (launched 2023, scale to 25k by 2025, replacing their paper reports)Muso and electronic vaccination registries in 2 districts. Logistics eLMIS piloted in some regions.DHIS2 Key barriers: rural electricity access (16% in 2020), poor internet, insecurity, paper shortages. National digital ambitions (DHIS2, DISC) exist, but rural CSCom patient recording remains paper-default, with digital limited to pilots and aggregation. No evidence of majority digital POS use.

revision_notes: Fetched the cited Health Data Collaborative Mopti case study and Gavi ZDLH Mali profile, confirming that patient forms and service registers at CSComs are paper-based, with only aggregated monthly data entered digitally into DHIS2 by facility staff. Found a peer-reviewed mixed-methods study (J Glob Health 2021, doi 10.7189/jogh.11.07003) of a DHIS2-tablet pilot for community health workers in Mopti, which found the paper-based system could not be eliminated even where tablets were introduced, due to Ministry of Health caution and connectivity constraints — CHWs used both in parallel. A May 2025 government meeting report states DISC-Mali (a national community health worker digitisation programme, first launched March 2023) has achieved 'digitalisation complète' of community-level essential care nationwide, and a 2024 Medic.org profile confirms individual CHWs now use tablets routinely for household visits. However, this digitisation is at the community/CHW layer that feeds into CSComs; individual patient registration and clinical records at the CSCom facility itself remain paper-based, with only monthly aggregate data entered into DHIS2 by facility staff (DTCs). This is consistent with the facility-level focus specified in the metadata guidance. Score confirmed at 2 (Mostly paper - some digital); insufficient evidence that facility-level (as opposed to community-level) capture has progressed to 'mostly digital'.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (CSComs) in Mali continue to rely predominantly on paper registers and individual client forms for recording patient encounters at the point of service. Community health workers (agents de santé communautaire) compile paper-based monthly reports, which facility staff (directeurs techniques du centre) review and enter as aggregated data into the national DHIS2 platform, in use since 2015-2016. A national community health worker digitisation programme, DISC-Mali (launched March 2023 using the Community Health Toolkit), has scaled tablet-based data capture for household-level community health visits, with a May 2025 government review describing this community layer as fully digitalised nationwide. However, this digitisation applies to community health worker activity rather than direct patient recording within the clinic itself, which remains largely paper-based, supplemented by digital aggregation of monthly statistics. Barriers including inconsistent electricity and connectivity in rural areas continue to constrain further digitisation at the facility level.
